extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, literary criticism, and humor theory; educated readers interested in theories of laughter and wit
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the distinct theoretical criteria for what produces comic laughter and wit as discussed in a scholarly history/critique of humor (mechanical, liberty, and Freudian accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful annoyances (not mere quantitative disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic laughter arises from 'playful annoyances' rather than from simple quantitative disappointments; we do not laugh at slight disappointments but at those extreme enough to 'rob us of the possibility of serious adjustment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with examples: a clown expected to leap who instead attends to an invisible grain (too little) versus his meticulous avoidance then sudden overreaction (too much) — both produce laughter because they function as playful annoyances that prevent normal adjustment. Note: degree matters; laughter appears when the annoyance crosses a threshold of absurdity or interference with expected action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation mismatch / 'psychic weight' (Lipps's theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is produced when what arrives is psychically lighter or heavier than what was expected — Lipps's idea of 'psychic weight' (e.g., expecting a cat but finding an aunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original formulation: comedy from expecting the psychically small and finding the psychically great (or vice versa). The author critiques the vagueness of 'psychic weight' and points out difficulties with mechanical accounts that force sequential causality rather than considering simultaneous collapse of expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite quantities / size-contrast incongruities
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts of magnitude (a small house in a row of palaces, a large baby among small ones) more readily provoke comic perception because the object crosses the range of our appetites and becomes preposterous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use size/scale contrast to create comic effect; but note the qualitative limit (enlarging a baby too much ceases to be a baby and becomes preposterous). This is an instance of quantitative incongruity producing comedy when it exceeds familiar bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release/liberty theory: laughter as removal of constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter results from a release of the nervous system from tension or constraint — 'a let-go,' a sudden relaxation of strain (Shaftesbury, Bain, Dewey, Penjon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulations: 'the Comic . . . starts from the Serious'; laughter as 'sudden relaxation of strain' or 'liberty visible.' This accounts for laughter when suspense or rigid constraint is removed (children freed from school). Critique: liberty explains many cases but is too negative and general to account for the unique 'humor tone' and does not uniquely predict laughter over other release behaviors (sigh, cough, walk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity/nature breaking constraints (Penjon/Freud linkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic speech/behavior can be 'the sudden eruption of a spontaneity,' where 'nature' (synonymous with liberty) breaks through the constraints of civilization producing humorous effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for understanding jokes and buffoonery as forms of revenge on constrainers or as brief escapes from mechanized mind. The author notes Freud draws on this idea as part of his broader unconscious-release account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor tone's uniqueness (not reducible to other reactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The feeling of the comic is a feeling of the comic und weiter nichts!' — the comic has a unique tone that cannot be fully explained by general conditions like release or relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution when applying broad mechanistic accounts (e.g., mere release) — many other actions follow release. Successful accounts must account for the distinct qualitative feeling of humorous laughter, not only the general removal of constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smile/laughter as positive instinctive function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and smiling can be positive expressions (e.g., Dewey's claim the infant's smile is an expression of assent) and thus part of positive functions or instincts with evolutionary utility, not merely mechanical by-products of release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to argue that some laughter is an active, semivoluntary behavior with social/communicative value rather than only a passive result of tension release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child play and nonsense as origin of wit (jest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud traces wit to child 'world-play' and 'thought-play': play with words/meanings that is pleasurable in its nonsense (Scherz) and which guards this pleasure against suppression by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'jest' is nonsense that makes sense only faintly; its value is the sheer folly — example: the professor who said 'I have the honor of seeing the Thirty Years' War!' — pleasurable in meaninglessness. This primitive playfulness underlies more elaborate forms of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit: nonsense that also has value/meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher wit combines the child's pleasure in nonsense with a meaningful statement — nonsense that lends glamour or protection to a sensible remark (Freud's distinction between 'jest' and 'wit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Heine's line about a millionaire treating someone 'as if I were an equal, quite famillionaire' — the nonsense highlights a sharper sense. Successful wit preserves play while providing sense/value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency wit: release of repressed impulses (aggressive/sexual)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mature class of wit (tendency wit) uses nonsense as a disguise to release repressed aggressive or sexual impulses from the unconscious, producing stronger, often uproarious laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud's central claim: when the underlying sense of a joke gratifies tendencies that would otherwise remain unfulfilled, the result is intense pleasure and laughter. Example: sexual/hostile implications masked by joking form. The author notes Freud's expansion of 'aggressive' to many social attacks and critiques over-generalization but accepts the core idea of release of repressed tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream–joke analogy: disguise and condensation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes resemble dreams in using condensation, displacement, ambiguity, opposites, word-twistings, and double meanings; dreams disguise forbidden thoughts to keep them out of consciousness, jokes disguise to let them in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics to employ for producing wit: double entendre, ambiguity, inverted order, semantic condensation. Use this to analyze how a witticism masks taboo content while permitting gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of psychic expenditure / condensation as source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud (following Lipps/Spencer) suggests wit produces pleasure via an 'unexpected economy of psychic expenditure' — a compressing or economizing tendency in which verbal/conceptual effort conveys more than its usual meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud analyzes many witticisms as instances of 'condensation' where psychic energy is economized. The author criticizes overreliance on this idea (gives an example where extracting meaning required more effort), but it remains a named criterion: perceived economy/condensation can enhance wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and reversal / preparedness and sudden fulfillment or disappointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic effect often depends on preparing psychic energy/expectation (set-up) and then delivering an unexpected arrival or deprivation — either a thwarting of desire or an achievement of the desired disaster — producing fresh laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the acrobat who repeatedly dodges apples (setting up expectation of nimble dodge) and then allows an apple to smash his skull produces renewed laughter; the man expecting a cat but finding aunt collapses preperceptions. Laughter can arise both from the deprivation of derision and from the deprivation of admiration — swapped roles still yield laughter.
